But there is also something else—a quiet satisfaction. 

I came here seeking experience, proving that my skills weren't just things learned from old books or family lore, but things I could *apply* in the messy reality of life on the frontier. I proved I can work, I proved I can see what needs fixing before it breaks, and I proved I value a community more than a quick payday. Rorie needed hands; he got them. Buttons needed care; he got that too.

But the cycle must continue. Stagnation is not mastery. To truly become one of those who can train others, I cannot simply be competent in the moment; I must be resilient over time. The road to Goldwise feels long, and my savings are thin, but I have a direction now—a confirmed path to earn coin under Jorj’s roof.

I will rest tonight. A proper night's sleep for myself, and quiet healing for Buttons. Tomorrow, the pack goes on again, and I pick up where I left off: moving forward, learning something new with every mile, and getting closer to becoming a ranger worthy of my own name.

She takes a slow breath, running her hand over the worn leather of her backpack, feeling the familiar weight of it—a weight that is no longer just supplies, but layers of unexpected experience.)*

The plan was clean: Highwater to Goldwise. A straight line toward Jorj’s harvest work, where coin could be earned and my skills refined by the demands of a structured job. I saw this summer as a necessary step—a rapid acquisition of utility before I returned home, armed with proven competence for the next generation.

But life in the country is rarely so tidy. The injury to Buttons forced me into a pause, a detour that stretched my intended path thin. Instead of rushing toward Goldwise, I found myself here, embedded in Rorie’s new world. 

I came seeking *payment*; I stayed for *purpose*.

The coin remains elusive—a stark reminder that hard work does not always translate to immediate silver, especially when you are offering your time and skill rather than just a physical labor exchange. But the ledger of my craft is full. The garden wasn't merely cleared; it was understood—the difference between good leaf and rank weed requires an eye for detail I must sharpen further. Helping with the roof wasn't just manual toil; it was an education in structural necessity, a practical lesson in what makes a home *sound*. 

And the oxen... that is where the true shift lies. My skill set listed 'Archery' and 'Survival,' but here, I have wrestled with patience and communication—the delicate balance of leading stubborn life. Training those green pairs has taught me more about the slow, persistent nature of mastery than any single day in the woods ever could.

I am tired. My body aches from hours spent between the bow, the shovel, and the yoke. The initial goal was to *arrive* at Goldwise; now, I have learned how to *inhabit* a place, how to provide value when payment is deferred. This detour hasn't been wasteful. It has simply redirected my definition of "keeping up." I am still on my path toward self-mastery, but the lessons are broader now—they encompass patience, community reliance, and the quiet dignity of honest labor, whether it’s felling trees or guiding a pair of oxen. The road to Goldwise is still there; perhaps I will arrive more whole for it than I left Highwater.

I am leaving not because I failed, but because I have gained what I needed: confidence in my ability to apply myself fully to whatever task lies before me—be it the delicate work of pruning a garden or the fierce focus required for tracking game.

The road back toward Goldwise, and eventually onward, is long. But now, when I look at that road, I don't just see distance; I see opportunities to refine what I have learned. The day I return home to Highwater, it won't be as a girl who left seeking adventure, but as someone with real knowledge—knowledge of the earth, animals, and the tenacity required to build a life from scratch. That is what I owe myself, and that is what I owe my village.

The road into Goldwise was meant to be a swift passage—a necessary transit between my small home and the promise of solid work. I came this summer armed with a list of connections and a clear objective: sharpen my craft, earn coin, and move on to Uncle Jorj’s harvest before the seasons turned. My mind was meticulously mapped out; every day should be dedicated to the forest—the tracking, the reading of the country, the perfect form of the draw. Self-mastery, I believed, required focus, a clean line between task and rest.

But the road has been far wider than my map allowed. 

The initial stop at Rorie’s homestead was meant to be a brief respite for Buttons' heel, a tactical delay. Instead, it became an unexpected anchor. The garden taught me that nature doesn't adhere to neat schedules; life is messy, and sometimes the most urgent work isn't with arrows, but with weeds. Roofing taught me that resilience requires more than just one strong back—it demands shared effort, a communal strength I hadn't anticipated needing.

And the harvest... staying through it felt less like a strategic delay and more like an inevitable pull of family. My plan was to be the focused ranger; my reality has been the practical helper.

I am still striving for mastery, but I see now that what I thought was "skill" on paper—perfect tracking, flawless archery—is only one facet of it. True competence, the kind I want to teach in Highwater, isn't just about the perfection of a single shot; it’s about the tenacity to keep working when your mount is lame, the patience to help mend a roof before winter sets in, and the grit to show up for family even when you are running on fumes.

The path to Goldwise remains my destination, but the journey here has been less of a straight line and more of a circle—a necessary detour into the life of these people who have welcomed me. I came looking only at my own reflection in the woods; I am leaving having learned how to look out for others within the community as well. The goal remains: return home, but now I carry with me not just the knowledge of survival, but a deeper understanding of endurance and connection.

The work is never done; it only changes form.
